cards.q: Talk for one minute: respond to the motion "Students should choose all of their own school subjects."

Concede the strongest point on the other side.

a: I'd argue against the motion, although I can see why it's appealing.

Even so, at fifteen, most of us simply don't know which subjects we'll need later, and dropping math or science too early could close doors.
Some might say we could always catch up later, but in practice that's far harder than it sounds.
So, while choice clearly matters, I'd still maintain that a strong core of shared subjects serves students better.

Some jobs, almost certainly. There's bound to be less demand for routine work like data entry, but new kinds of jobs will probably appear as well, as they have with every major technology.

cards.q: Why do you think so many teenagers sleep badly these days?
a: Phones are probably the main cause, since the light from screens can keep the brain alert late at night. Exam pressure may well play a part too, although it likely varies from person to person.

I'd say it's partly biological, because teenagers' body clocks naturally shift later. Combine that with early starts and late-night scrolling, and it's hardly surprising that so many of us are exhausted.

cards.q: What's the difference between weather and climate? Isn't it the same thing?
a: The key difference is that weather changes from day to day, whereas climate is the usual pattern over thirty years or more. So a sandstorm tomorrow is weather, but summers getting hotter decade after decade is a sign of climate change.

They're related, but not the same. In everyday terms, weather is like your mood on one particular day, while climate is more like your personality, which is why one rainy week in Riyadh doesn't mean the climate has changed.

cards.q: Talk for one minute: explain your science project on growing plants with less water to a parent who isn't a scientist.
steps: Link it to something they already know.

a: You know how farms have thin black pipes running along the ground under the palm trees? Well, my project builds on that idea.
The technical term is drip irrigation, but basically, it means giving each plant small amounts of water right at its roots.
The water travels slowly through the pipes and drips out through tiny holes, so very little is lost to the sun or the wind.
Unlike a sprinkler, which sprays the whole area, a drip system only waters the soil where the roots actually are.
It matters because water is scarce here, and farms use far more of it than homes do.
